questions.q: Why does this lesson say reference data governance needs its own mechanics, separate from master data governance?
options: Because a reference data change can silently affect every system that stores the changed code, unlike a master data change affecting one record
Because reference data is never actually governed in practice
Because reference data changes require no approval of any kind
Because reference data is always larger in volume than master data
questions.explain: Updating one customer's address affects that record; redefining what a status code means can ripple across every transactional system that stores that code.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a reference data steward from a master data owner?
options: A steward's scope is narrower and more operational, often held by someone close to the specific business process the code list supports
A steward has no accountability at all, unlike a data owner
A steward and a data owner are exactly the same role with different titles
A steward only exists for external, standards-based reference data
questions.explain: A data owner answers whether a whole record is correct; a steward answers whether a specific code list is internally consistent and safe for every consuming system — often filled by a business-process expert like a finance analyst for a chart of accounts.

questions.q: What should a reference data change request document, according to this lesson?
options: The specific code change, the business reason, which systems consume the list, the effective date, and how historical data is handled
Only the name of the employee requesting the change
Nothing beyond the new code itself — no other documentation is needed
The total storage size of the reference data table
questions.explain: Skipping any of these elements is how a reference data change becomes an incident instead of a routine, well-communicated update.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff between centralized and distributed reference data management, per this lesson?
options: Centralized management maximizes consistency but can bottleneck; distributed management keeps domain expertise close but risks uneven rigor
Centralized management is always faster with no downsides
Distributed management eliminates the need for any change-request process
There is no meaningful tradeoff between the two approaches
questions.explain: One source of truth under centralized management is consistent but can become a bottleneck; distributing ownership scales better but risks some business areas treating the process as optional.

questions.q: What structure do most mature reference data governance programs land on, according to this lesson?
options: A hybrid of central tooling and shared process, with distributed stewards who own the actual content decisions
Pure centralization with no business-area input whatsoever
Pure distribution with no shared process or tooling at all
A rotating committee that changes ownership every month
questions.explain: This hybrid echoes the hybrid MDM architecture style covered earlier in the course — shared infrastructure and process, with domain-specific ownership of content decisions.
